title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
description: Grade 11 Biology: the human respiratory system, the mechanism of breathing, exchange and transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, and respiratory disorders.

topics.title: The Human Respiratory System and Mechanism of Breathing
topics.concept:
Every cell needs oxygen to release energy from food, and produces carbon dioxide as a waste. The process of taking in oxygen-rich air and giving out carbon-dioxide-rich air is breathing (ventilation), while the actual release of energy inside the cells is cellular respiration.

Air travels through the human respiratory system in this order: nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea (windpipe) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The two lungs sit in the chest (thoracic cavity), protected by the ribs and separated from the abdomen by a dome-shaped muscle, the diaphragm. The trachea is kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. The actual exchange of gases takes place in millions of tiny balloon-like air sacs called alveoli, which have very thin walls and a rich network of blood capillaries.

Breathing has two steps:

  • Inspiration (breathing in): the diaphragm flattens (moves down) and the rib muscles raise the ribs, so the chest cavity enlarges. The pressure inside the lungs falls below the outside air, and air rushes in.
  • Expiration (breathing out): the diaphragm and rib muscles relax, the chest cavity shrinks, pressure inside rises, and air is pushed out.

So breathing works by changing the volume and pressure of the chest. The rate and depth of breathing are controlled automatically by the respiratory centre in the brain.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name, in order, the parts through which air passes to reach the lungs.
examples.solution:
Trace the air path.

  • Nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
examples.answer: Nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

examples.problem: Example 2: Where does the actual exchange of gases take place, and why is it suited for this?
examples.solution:
Gas exchange happens in tiny sacs.

  • In the alveoli of the lungs.
  • They have very thin walls and a rich blood supply, ideal for gas exchange.
examples.answer: In the alveoli, which have thin walls and a rich capillary network — perfect for gas exchange.

examples.problem: Example 3: What happens to the diaphragm and chest cavity during inspiration?
examples.solution:
Think about volume and pressure.

  • The diaphragm flattens (moves down) and the chest cavity enlarges.
  • Pressure inside falls, so air rushes in.
examples.answer: The diaphragm flattens and the chest cavity enlarges, lowering the pressure so air rushes in.

recap:
• Air path: nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
  • Gas exchange in the thin-walled, capillary-rich alveoli; diaphragm + rib muscles drive breathing.
  • Inspiration: diaphragm flattens, chest enlarges, pressure falls, air in.
  • Expiration: muscles relax, chest shrinks, pressure rises, air out.

quiz.q: The actual exchange of gases in the lungs takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: The thin-walled alveoli are the site of gas exchange.
The diaphragm flattens during inspiration, enlarging the chest cavity.

topics.title: Exchange and Transport of Gases
topics.concept:
Once fresh air reaches the alveoli, gases move between the air and the blood by simple diffusion — each gas moves from where it is in higher concentration (pressure) to where it is lower. In the alveoli, oxygen is high and carbon dioxide is low; in the blood arriving from the body it is the opposite. So:

  • Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood.
  • Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli, to be breathed out.

The blood then carries these gases around the body.

Transport of oxygen: most oxygen (about 97%) is carried by the red pigment haemoglobin in the red blood cells, forming oxyhaemoglobin. Each haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs (where oxygen is high) and releases it in the tissues (where oxygen is low). A small amount of oxygen is also dissolved in the plasma.

Transport of carbon dioxide: CO₂ is carried in three ways — mostly as bicarbonate ions dissolved in the plasma (about 70%), some bound to haemoglobin (as carbaminohaemoglobin), and a little dissolved directly in the plasma. In the lungs, the CO₂ is released from the blood into the alveoli and exhaled. This neat two-way exchange keeps supplying cells with oxygen and clearing away their carbon dioxide.

examples.problem: Example 1: By what process do gases move between the alveoli and the blood?
examples.solution:
No energy is used.

  • By simple diffusion, from higher to lower concentration (pressure).
examples.answer: By diffusion, each gas moving from higher to lower concentration (partial pressure).

examples.problem: Example 2: How is most oxygen carried in the blood?
examples.solution:
Oxygen binds a red pigment.

  • About 97% of oxygen is carried by haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin.
examples.answer: Most oxygen (about 97%) is carried bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin.

examples.problem: Example 3: In what main form is carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
examples.solution:
CO₂ has several forms; one dominates.

  • Most CO₂ (about 70%) is carried as bicarbonate ions in the plasma.
examples.answer: Mostly as bicarbonate ions dissolved in the plasma (about 70%).

recap:
• Gases exchange by diffusion: O₂ alveoli → blood; CO₂ blood → alveoli.
  • Oxygen: ~97% on haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin); rest dissolved in plasma.
  • CO₂: ~70% as bicarbonate, some as carbaminohaemoglobin, a little dissolved.
  • O₂ loaded in lungs, released in tissues; CO₂ the reverse.

quiz.q: Most oxygen is transported in the blood by:
quiz.explanation: About 97% of oxygen binds to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin.

quiz.q: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as:
quiz.explanation: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate ions in the plasma.

topics.title: Respiratory Disorders and Lung Health
topics.concept:
The respiratory system can be affected by infections, pollution and tobacco smoke. Knowing the common disorders helps us protect our lungs. Some important respiratory disorders:

  • Asthma — the bronchi and bronchioles narrow and swell, causing difficulty in breathing, wheezing and coughing. It is often triggered by allergies, dust or cold air.
  • Bronchitis — inflammation of the bronchi, with a persistent cough and mucus, often linked to smoking or pollution.
  • Emphysema — the walls of the alveoli are damaged and break down, reducing the surface area for gas exchange; cigarette smoking is a major cause.
  • Pneumonia — an infection in which the alveoli fill with fluid, making breathing hard.
  • Occupational lung diseases — caused by breathing harmful dust at work, such as silicosis (stone/sand dust) and asbestosis (asbestos fibres).

Smoking is the single biggest avoidable cause of lung damage and lung cancer; the smoke contains many harmful chemicals, including nicotine and tar. Air pollution also damages the lungs. To keep the respiratory system healthy: avoid smoking and smoky places, reduce exposure to dust and pollution (wear a mask where needed), keep indoor air clean, and exercise to strengthen the breathing muscles. Vaccination and prompt treatment of infections also protect the lungs.

examples.problem: Example 1: What happens to the airways in asthma?
examples.solution:
It affects the bronchi and bronchioles.

  • They narrow and swell, making breathing difficult (wheezing, coughing).
examples.answer: The bronchi and bronchioles narrow and swell, causing difficulty in breathing (wheezing, coughing).

examples.problem: Example 2: Name a respiratory disease strongly linked to cigarette smoking.
examples.solution:
Smoking damages the alveoli.

  • Emphysema (also bronchitis and lung cancer) is strongly linked to smoking.
examples.answer: Emphysema (also chronic bronchitis and lung cancer).

examples.problem: Example 3: State two ways to keep the respiratory system healthy.
examples.solution:
Reduce harm and strengthen the lungs.

  • Avoid smoking and smoky places; reduce dust and pollution exposure.
  • Exercise to strengthen breathing muscles.
examples.answer: Avoid smoking and air pollution (use a mask where needed), and exercise to strengthen the breathing muscles.

recap:
• Asthma: narrowed, swollen airways; bronchitis: inflamed bronchi; emphysema: damaged alveoli (smoking).
  • Pneumonia: alveoli fill with fluid; occupational diseases: silicosis, asbestosis.
  • Smoking = biggest avoidable cause of lung damage/cancer; pollution also harms.
  • Protect lungs: no smoking, less dust/pollution, exercise, vaccination.

quiz.q: A disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged, often by smoking, is:
quiz.explanation: Emphysema is the breakdown of alveolar walls, strongly linked to smoking.

quiz.q: An occupational lung disease caused by breathing stone/sand dust is:
quiz.explanation: Silicosis results from inhaling silica (stone/sand) dust at work.

questions.q: Taking in oxygen-rich air and giving out CO₂-rich air is called:
questions.explanation: Breathing (ventilation) is the exchange of air with the environment.

questions.q: The windpipe is also called the:
questions.explanation: The trachea is the windpipe.

questions.q: The dome-shaped muscle that helps in breathing is the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm separates the chest from the abdomen and aids breathing.

questions.q: Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the:
questions.explanation: The alveoli are the site of gas exchange.

questions.q: The trachea is kept open by rings of:
questions.explanation: C-shaped cartilage rings keep the trachea open.

questions.q: During inspiration, the chest cavity:
questions.explanation: The chest cavity enlarges during inspiration, lowering pressure.

questions.q: Gases move between alveoli and blood by:
questions.explanation: Gases diffuse from higher to lower partial pressure.

questions.q: Most oxygen in the blood is carried by:
questions.explanation: About 97% of oxygen binds haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.q: Oxygen combined with haemoglobin is called:
questions.explanation: Oxygen + haemoglobin = oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.q: Most carbon dioxide is transported as:
questions.explanation: About 70% of CO₂ travels as bicarbonate ions in the plasma.

questions.q: In the tissues, oxyhaemoglobin tends to:
questions.explanation: Where oxygen is low (tissues), haemoglobin releases its oxygen.

questions.q: A disorder with narrowed, swollen airways and wheezing is:
questions.explanation: Asthma narrows and inflames the airways.

questions.q: Damage to the alveolar walls, often from smoking, is:
questions.explanation: Emphysema is breakdown of alveolar walls due to smoking.

questions.q: Silicosis and asbestosis are examples of:
questions.explanation: They are occupational lung diseases from inhaling harmful dust.

questions.q: The single biggest avoidable cause of lung damage is:
questions.explanation: Smoking is the leading avoidable cause of lung damage and cancer.

questions.q: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood because in the alveoli the oxygen level is:
options: Higher than in the incoming blood
questions.explanation: Diffusion runs from high to low; alveolar O₂ is higher than in the venous blood, so O₂ moves into the blood.

questions.q: Haemoglobin is well suited to its job because it picks up oxygen where O₂ is ____ and releases it where O₂ is ____.
questions.explanation: It loads O₂ in the high-oxygen lungs and unloads it in the low-oxygen tissues.

questions.q: Carbon-monoxide poisoning is dangerous mainly because CO:
options: Binds haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does
questions.explanation: CO binds haemoglobin far more tightly than O₂, blocking oxygen transport.

questions.q: Emphysema reduces gas exchange chiefly because the breakdown of alveolar walls:
options: Decreases the surface area for diffusion
questions.explanation: Fewer, larger air spaces mean less surface area, so less oxygen can be absorbed.

questions.q: Breathing rate increases during exercise mainly to:
options: Supply more oxygen and remove more CO₂
questions.explanation: Active muscles need more O₂ and produce more CO₂, so ventilation rises.

questions.q: A worker constantly exposed to fine stone dust without a mask is at risk of:
questions.explanation: Inhaled silica dust scars the lungs, causing silicosis — an occupational disease.
